topic: PostgreSQL at depth: planner, indexes, EXPLAIN, locks, transactions, window functions
why: On almost every engagement the customer's Postgres (RDS, Cloud SQL, or a VM their DBA guards) is the shared dependency your feature lands on, and the new access patterns you introduce (per-tenant filters, JSONB metadata, event tables, job queues, embeddings side tables) are what turns 'the AI thing is slow' into a P1 with your name on it. You will be asked to read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a screen-share in front of their DBA and propose an index they will accept, and to ship a schema change to a multi-billion-row table with no maintenance window. Knowing the planner, MVCC and the lock table cold is what lets you say 'this will take 40 seconds and block nothing' and be right.
prerequisites: SQL fluency: joins, GROUP BY, HAVING, subqueries, basic DDL and DML; the pgexercises Basic and Joins sets should feel like warm-up, not learning

A running Dokeo with real tables from topics 25 and 26 (Production Python architecture; FastAPI in production), plus the ability to generate 5-10M rows of skewed seed data with generate_series so plans actually change
Topic 14 (AWS data: RDS Postgres) for parameter groups, shared_preload_libraries on managed Postgres, Performance Insights and where slow-query logs land
Topic 3 (Performance and troubleshooting on a single box) so 'random_page_cost', 'page cache' and 'spilled to disk' map to iostat, vmstat and real hardware
Docker: run postgres:16 with a named volume and custom postgresql.conf flags (-c shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements,auto_explain), psql with \timing, \x and \watch
Topic 21 (Observability) is helpful, not required, for wiring pg_stat_statements and lock waits into Grafana

subtopics.name: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE line by line
subtopics.learn: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, SETTINGS, WAL, FORMAT TEXT|JSON) and read a plan tree bottom-up and inner-to-outer: cost=startup..total, rows and width are estimates; actual time=first..last, rows and loops are measured, and a child's actual rows must be multiplied by loops to get the true row count. Hunt for the first node where estimated rows diverges from actual by more than 10x, for Filter and Rows Removed by Filter (rows fetched then thrown away), for Buffers: shared hit vs read vs dirtied and temp read/written (a Sort or Hash that spilled), and for Planning Time vs Execution Time. Know that EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the statement, so wrap INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK, that TIMING adds overhead on high-node-count plans (use TIMING OFF for a fair measurement), and that BUFFERS is only on by default from PostgreSQL 18. Paste the same plan into explain.depesz.com or explain.dalibo.com when it is more than a screen long, but be able to read raw text when the customer's laptop has no internet.

subtopics.name: The cost model and the planner knobs that actually matter
subtopics.learn: Understand the arbitrary-unit cost model: seq_page_cost 1.0, random_page_cost 4.0 (drop to 1.1 on SSD/EBS gp3 or the planner will avoid index scans on big tables), cpu_tuple_cost 0.01, cpu_index_tuple_cost 0.005, cpu_operator_cost 0.0025, and effective_cache_size (a hint about OS cache, default 4GB, set to ~50-75% of RAM) which makes index scans look cheaper without allocating anything. Know work_mem (per sort/hash node, per query, default 4MB; set per session with SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB' for a known-heavy report rather than globally) and hash_mem_multiplier, and when JIT (jit_above_cost 100000) adds seconds of compile time to a plan that would have run in milliseconds. Use enable_seqscan/enable_nestloop/enable_hashjoin = off only as a diagnostic to see the plan the optimizer rejected and what it costed it at, never in production, and read the SETTINGS block in EXPLAIN to see which non-default knobs were in play on the customer's box.

subtopics.name: Statistics, ANALYZE and the anatomy of a misestimate
subtopics.learn: Read pg_stats for a column: null_frac, n_distinct (negative means a fraction of rows), most_common_vals/most_common_freqs, histogram_bounds and correlation (near 1 or -1 means index range scans are cheap sequential IO). Know that default_statistics_target 100 samples 30000 rows and gives 100 MCVs/histogram buckets, that a skewed tenant_id column with 5000 distinct values needs ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN tenant_id SET STATISTICS 1000 followed by ANALYZE, and that autovacuum only re-analyzes after autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor (10%) of the table changes, so a freshly bulk-loaded table is planned on empty-table stats until you run ANALYZE yourself. Fix correlated-column misestimates (city implies country, status implies is_closed) with CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) ON a, b FROM t, and recognise the unfixable ones: functions on columns, JSONB path expressions and inequality on parameters all default to fixed selectivity guesses (0.005, 0.333) regardless of data.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Statistics Used by the Planner

subtopics.name: B-tree anatomy and the column-order rule
subtopics.learn: Picture the B-tree: a balanced tree of 8kB pages whose leaf level is a doubly linked list of sorted (key, ctid) entries, so every lookup is O(log n) page reads to a leaf followed by a sequential walk along leaves, and every row visit from the leaf is a random heap read. Internalise the concatenated-index rule: the index is sorted by column 1, then column 2 within equal column 1, so equality predicates go first and the single range or ORDER BY column goes last; (tenant_id, created_at) serves WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND created_at > $2 ORDER BY created_at with one range walk, while (created_at, tenant_id) has to scan every tenant's rows in the date range and filter. Distinguish Index Cond (used to navigate the tree) from Filter (evaluated on each row fetched) in the plan, and know why a leading column not in the WHERE clause makes the index unusable except for the rarely-chosen skip-scan-like full index scan.

resource.label: Use The Index, Luke - Concatenated Indexes (column order)

subtopics.name: Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap scans and when each fires
subtopics.learn: Predict the scan type from selectivity and correlation: Seq Scan for anything past roughly 5-10% of a large table (and always for tiny tables), Index Scan for a handful of rows, Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan for the middle ground where the planner sorts matching ctids by page to turn random IO into sequential IO (look for Recheck Cond and Heap Blocks: exact=N lossy=M; lossy means the bitmap exceeded work_mem and whole pages were rechecked). Understand Index Only Scan needs every referenced column in the index (add non-key columns with INCLUDE) and a visibility map bit set for each page, otherwise it reports Heap Fetches: N and costs the same as an Index Scan; freshly loaded or heavily updated tables have unset VM bits until VACUUM runs, which is why the same index is fast on Monday and slow on Friday. Know how BitmapAnd/BitmapOr combine two single-column indexes, and why a composite index still beats them for a hot query.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes

subtopics.name: Partial, expression, covering and ordered indexes
subtopics.learn: Build each shape and prove it is used: a partial index CREATE INDEX ... ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending' is tiny and stays hot, but the planner only picks it when it can prove the query predicate implies the index predicate, so a parameterised status = $1 executed as a generic plan will skip it; an expression index ON users (lower(email)) is required when the ORM emits WHERE lower(email) = lower($1) (a plain index on email is useless there, see Use The Index Luke's 'obfuscation' chapter); INCLUDE (payload_size) turns an Index Scan plus heap fetch into an Index Only Scan for a read-heavy path without widening the key. Match index order to ORDER BY: a B-tree can be walked backwards, so (tenant_id, created_at) serves ORDER BY created_at DESC, but ORDER BY created_at DESC, id ASC needs (created_at DESC, id ASC) explicitly, and NULLS FIRST/LAST must match too. Check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan before dropping an index the customer swears is used.

subtopics.name: GIN, GiST, BRIN and hash: indexing JSONB, text search, arrays and time series
subtopics.learn: Choose the non-B-tree index by operator: GIN on a jsonb column with the default jsonb_ops supports @>, ?, ?|, ?& and key-existence, while jsonb_path_ops is roughly 3x smaller and faster but only supports @>; a B-tree on an extracted path ((metadata->>'customer_id')) beats both for equality on one known key. Use GIN with pg_trgm's gin_trgm_ops for LIKE '%term%' and ILIKE (the only way those get an index) and GIN on a stored tsvector generated column for full-text search; know GIN's fastupdate pending list (gin_pending_list_limit, 4MB) makes inserts cheap but the first query after a burst pays to merge it. Use BRIN (pages_per_range 128) on append-only, physically ordered columns like created_at on an events table: a few kB instead of GBs, but useless once updates and deletes scramble physical order. GiST is for ranges, geometry and EXCLUDE constraints (no overlapping bookings); hash indexes are equality-only and rarely worth it over B-tree.

subtopics.name: Join algorithms: Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join and how misestimates pick the wrong one
subtopics.learn: Know the three algorithms and their sweet spots: Nested Loop with an inner Index Scan is ideal when the outer side is small (a handful of rows) and catastrophic when the planner estimated rows=1 but got 50000, because the inner scan runs 50000 times (loops=50000 in the plan); Hash Join builds an in-memory hash on the smaller input (Batches: 1 is good, Batches: 16 means it spilled to disk because the build side exceeded work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier); Merge Join needs both inputs sorted and wins when indexes already provide the order or both sides are huge. Read Hash Cond, Merge Cond and Join Filter, and know the planner only considers all join orders up to join_collapse_limit/from_collapse_limit (8) and switches to the genetic optimizer above geqo_threshold (12) tables, so a 14-table ORM join is planned heuristically. Recognise parallel plans (Gather, Parallel Seq Scan, Parallel Hash Join; max_parallel_workers_per_gather default 2) and why a query that ran in parallel on your laptop runs serially on a 2-vCPU RDS instance.

resource.label: Use The Index, Luke - The Join Operation

subtopics.name: Sorting, LIMIT, top-N and keyset pagination
subtopics.learn: Read Sort Method: quicksort Memory: NkB (fine), external merge Disk: NkB (spilled: raise work_mem for the session or provide the order via an index), and top-N heapsort (a LIMIT let the sort keep only N rows). Know that an index whose order matches ORDER BY lets a LIMIT 20 stop after 20 index entries (Index Scan with no Sort node at all), that Incremental Sort (PG13+) can exploit a partial prefix match (Presorted Key), and that OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20 must produce and discard 100000 rows every page so admin exports and infinite scroll get slower per page until they time out. Replace it with keyset pagination: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 with WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) using row-value comparison, which walks the (created_at DESC, id DESC) index directly and is stable under concurrent inserts.

resource.label: Use The Index, Luke - Fetching the next page (keyset pagination)

subtopics.name: Finding the slow queries: pg_stat_statements, auto_explain and the slow log
subtopics.learn: Enable shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements,auto_explain' (a restart; on RDS via the parameter group) and CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements, then rank by total_exec_time (what burns the box), by mean_exec_time (what users feel) and by calls (N+1 candidates), reading shared_blks_read, temp_blks_written and wal_bytes per statement; normalised queryid lets you join to auto_explain output and to pg_stat_activity.query_id when compute_query_id = auto. Configure auto_explain.log_min_duration = '250ms', log_analyze = on, log_buffers = on, log_timing = off (timing on every node is expensive), log_nested_statements = on for functions, log_format = json and sample_rate < 1 on busy systems, so the plan that was slow in production is captured with the parameter values that made it slow, which is exactly what you cannot reproduce by hand. Set log_min_duration_statement, log_lock_waits = on and log_temp_files = 0 as the baseline on every customer database you touch, and call pg_stat_statements_reset() at the start of a measurement window rather than reading lifetime averages.

subtopics.name: MVCC: tuple versions, snapshots, dead tuples and HOT updates
subtopics.learn: Understand that every row version carries xmin (creating transaction), xmax (deleting or updating transaction) and ctid, that a snapshot decides visibility per transaction, and that UPDATE never modifies in place: it writes a new version and marks the old one dead, so an update-heavy table is a delete-heavy table. Know the HOT (heap-only tuple) optimisation: when no indexed column changes and the page has free space (leave room with ALTER TABLE t SET (fillfactor = 90)), the new version is chained inside the page and no index entries are written; watch n_tup_hot_upd vs n_tup_upd in pg_stat_user_tables to see whether an 'updated_at' index is silently defeating it. Understand why a transaction left open for hours (state = 'idle in transaction' in pg_stat_activity, backend_xmin far behind) pins every dead tuple since it began across the entire database, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and know the 2^31 transaction-ID wraparound story well enough to explain autovacuum_freeze_max_age and why 'database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound' is the outage you never want to be on-site for.

subtopics.name: VACUUM, autovacuum tuning and diagnosing bloat
subtopics.learn: Know the trigger math: autovacuum vacuums a table when dead tuples exceed autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (0.2) times reltuples, so a 500M-row table waits for 100M dead rows; fix it per table with ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 50000) and, for append-only tables, autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor so the visibility map gets set. Understand that autovacuum is throttled by autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay (2ms) and cost_limit (200), that three workers (autovacuum_max_workers) can be starved by one huge table, and that cancelled autovacuums (log line 'canceling autovacuum task') come from DDL and lock conflicts. Measure bloat with pgstattuple (dead_tuple_percent, free_percent) or the pg_stat_user_tables n_dead_tup/n_live_tup ratio, watch pg_stat_progress_vacuum during a long run, and know your repair options ranked by lock cost: plain VACUUM (no exclusive lock, does not return space to the OS), REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY for index bloat, pg_repack for online table rewrite, VACUUM FULL only with an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and a maintenance window.

subtopics.name: Isolation levels, lost updates, write skew and the 40001 retry contract
subtopics.learn: Demonstrate each level in two psql sessions: READ COMMITTED (the default) takes a fresh snapshot per statement, so a read-modify-write in application code (SELECT balance; compute; UPDATE) loses updates, while a single UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 is safe because UPDATE re-reads the latest committed version of the row; REPEATABLE READ takes one snapshot per transaction and aborts a writer that touches a row modified since with SQLSTATE 40001; SERIALIZABLE adds SSI predicate locks (SIReadLock in pg_locks) and detects write skew such as two on-call doctors both reading 'two on call' and both leaving. Know the retry contract: any code that uses REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE must catch 40001 and rerun the whole transaction with backoff, and be able to choose between the pessimistic tools (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE, and how FK checks take FOR KEY SHARE on the parent row) and optimistic ones (a version column with UPDATE ... WHERE version = $1, or SERIALIZABLE) based on contention and transaction length.

subtopics.name: Lock modes, the lock queue, deadlocks and reading pg_locks
subtopics.learn: Memorise the table-level lock ladder and which statement takes which: SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE take ROW EXCLUSIVE, VACUUM and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY take SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, plain CREATE INDEX takes SHARE (blocks writes), and most ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE and VACUUM FULL take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE which conflicts with everything including SELECT. Understand the killer property: lock requests queue FIFO, so an ALTER TABLE waiting behind one long SELECT blocks every subsequent SELECT on that table too, which is why every migration session must SET lock_timeout = '3s' and retry rather than wait. Diagnose live with pg_stat_activity (wait_event_type = 'Lock', wait_event relation/transactionid/tuple), pg_blocking_pids(pid) to find the head of the chain, pg_locks joined on pid and granted = false, and pg_cancel_backend/pg_terminate_backend to break it; reproduce a deadlock (two sessions updating rows in opposite order) and read the deadlock_timeout (1s) detector's error, which names both queries. Implement a job queue correctly with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1 and know when NOWAIT or advisory locks (pg_try_advisory_xact_lock) are the better tool.

subtopics.name: Zero-downtime schema changes on live tables
subtopics.learn: Build a checklist of what rewrites, what scans and what is metadata-only: ADD COLUMN with a constant DEFAULT (even NOT NULL) is instant since PG11 (attmissingval), a volatile default such as clock_timestamp() rewrites the table; adding NOT NULL to an existing column scans under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, so instead ADD CONSTRAINT c CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT c (SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, concurrent writes allowed), then SET NOT NULL which PG12+ skips the scan for because a valid CHECK exists; ADD FOREIGN KEY ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE follows the same pattern; varchar(n) to text is metadata-only, int to bigint is a rewrite you do with a new column, a trigger or batched backfill, and a swap. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (two table scans, waits for every transaction that could see the table, cannot run inside a transaction block, so your migration tool must run it outside BEGIN), check pg_index.indisvalid afterwards because a failed or cancelled build leaves an INVALID index that writes still maintain and the planner ignores, and drop it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Wrap every DDL in SET lock_timeout = '3s' with an exponential-backoff retry loop, and create primary keys on big tables as CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY followed by ALTER TABLE ... ADD PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - ALTER TABLE (Notes section on locking and rewrites)

subtopics.name: Window functions: frames, ranking, lag/lead and latest-per-key
subtopics.learn: Write OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o frame) fluently and know the default frame trap: with ORDER BY and no frame clause the frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes peer rows with equal ORDER BY values, so a running sum over dates with ties jumps in steps; use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for true row-by-row totals, ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a 7-row moving average, GROUPS (PG11+) for peer groups, and EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW where needed. Use row_number(), rank(), dense_rank(), ntile(), lag(x, 1, default)/lead() for gap and change detection, first_value() and last_value() (last_value needs a frame ending at UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING or it returns the current row), FILTER (WHERE ...) on aggregates, and a named WINDOW w AS (...) clause to avoid repetition. Know that window results cannot be referenced in WHERE (wrap in a subquery or CTE), that a WindowAgg node requires a Sort unless an index on (p, o) provides the order, and compare row_number() = 1 against DISTINCT ON (device_id) ... ORDER BY device_id, ts DESC and LATERAL for the latest-per-key problem you will write on every telemetry engagement.

subtopics.name: CTEs, materialization fences, recursive queries and LATERAL rewrites
subtopics.learn: Know that since PG12 a non-recursive CTE referenced once is inlined into the parent query and optimised with it, that WITH x AS MATERIALIZED forces the old optimisation fence (useful to pin a good plan or to force a filter to happen first), that NOT MATERIALIZED inlines even a multiply-referenced CTE, and that CTEs containing INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ... RETURNING are always materialised and run exactly once. Write WITH RECURSIVE for org charts and dependency trees, understand UNION vs UNION ALL cycle behaviour and the PG14+ CYCLE and SEARCH DEPTH FIRST clauses, and cap depth defensively. Master the rewrites that fix real slow queries: LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE d.device_id = x.id ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1) for top-N per group hitting an index once per outer row; NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN (NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields a single NULL, and cannot become an anti-join); WHERE a = $1 OR b = $1 split into UNION ALL when the planner will not use BitmapOr; and col = ANY($1::int[]) instead of a 2000-item IN list.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)

subtopics.name: Declarative partitioning and partition pruning
subtopics.learn: Partition when a table is large and queries carry the partition key: PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) monthly for events and audit logs, LIST (tenant_id) for a few huge tenants, HASH when you only need to spread. Verify pruning in EXPLAIN (only the matching partitions appear; Subplans Removed: N shows execution-time pruning for parameters and nested loops; enable_partition_pruning must be on) and know the constraints: the partition key must be part of every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint, indexes created on the parent cascade to partitions, ATTACH PARTITION scans the new table unless it already carries a matching CHECK constraint, and DETACH PARTITION CONCURRENTLY (PG14+) avoids the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Understand the operational win (DROP or DETACH an old partition instead of a DELETE that creates months of bloat and vacuum work, use pg_partman or a cron to pre-create partitions) and the cost: planning time grows with partition count, thousands of partitions hurt every query, and partition-wise joins and aggregates are off by default (enable_partitionwise_join).

subtopics.name: Connections, PgBouncer transaction mode and the prepared-statement plan cache
subtopics.learn: Understand that every connection is a forked backend process (several MB of memory plus lock-table and snapshot overhead), that max_connections = 500 on a 4-vCPU RDS instance is a cry for help, and that PgBouncer in pool_mode = transaction is the standard fix but breaks anything session-scoped: SET (use SET LOCAL), server-side prepared statements (until PgBouncer 1.21's max_prepared_statements, or disable the driver cache with asyncpg statement_cache_size=0 / psycopg prepare_threshold=None), LISTEN/NOTIFY, session advisory locks, temp tables and WITH HOLD cursors; size default_pool_size to roughly (2 x cores) + spindles on the server side and let clients queue. Know the plan_cache_mode behaviour for prepared statements: five custom plans, then a generic plan if it is not costlier on average, which is how a skewed tenant_id gets the small-tenant plan forever (force_custom_plan fixes it at the cost of re-planning). Round out the write path: synchronous_commit = off per transaction for non-critical writes (risk: lose the last ~600ms on crash, never corruption), INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE/DO NOTHING for idempotent ingestion, and COPY FROM STDIN rather than batched INSERTs for bulk loads.

outcomes: You can take an unfamiliar EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output for a five-table join and, within three minutes and without tooling, point at the node where estimated rows diverges from actual rows by more than 10x, name the cause (stale statistics, correlated columns, function on a column, generic plan, missing extended statistics) and state the change that fixes it.

You can, for WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 on a 10M-row table, write the single index (column order, partial predicate, INCLUDE columns, direction) that yields an Index Scan or Index Only Scan with no Sort node and Heap Fetches: 0, and prove it with the before and after plans.

You can generate 5-10M rows of Zipf-skewed multi-tenant seed data with generate_series, take three real Dokeo queries from seconds to under 5 ms, and explain every line of each before/after plan including Buffers and Sort Method.

You can add a NOT NULL column, a foreign key and a unique index to a 10M-row table while pgbench -c 16 writes to it, with zero failed client transactions and no lock wait above one second, using CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID/VALIDATE, and a lock_timeout retry wrapper, and read the lock modes each step took from pg_locks while it runs.

You can reproduce a deadlock, a lock-queue pile-up behind an ALTER TABLE, and an INVALID index in two or three psql sessions, then diagnose each from pg_stat_activity, pg_blocking_pids() and pg_locks alone and state what every session holds and waits on.

You can write a lost-update demonstration in READ COMMITTED, show it becomes a 40001 under REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, implement the retry loop, and justify which of atomic UPDATE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, a version column, or SERIALIZABLE is right for a given contention profile.

You can write latest-row-per-key, 7-day moving average, gap detection and top-N-per-group three ways each (window function, DISTINCT ON, LATERAL) and say which one the planner executes without a Sort given a specific index.

You can read pg_stat_statements on a customer database, rank by total_exec_time and by mean_exec_time x calls with shared_blks_read, defend the choice of the three statements worth fixing in a 10-minute conversation with their DBA, and configure auto_explain so the next slow plan is captured with its real parameters.
failureModes: A 500M-row events table keeps the default autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor of 0.2 while a nightly analytics job holds a transaction open for six hours; vacuum cannot clear anything behind that backend_xmin, the table reaches 3x bloat, every Index Only Scan reports thousands of Heap Fetches, p99 climbs weekly and the customer's response is to buy a larger instance.

The ORM emits WHERE lower(email) = lower($1) against a table with a plain B-tree on email; the plan is a 20M-row Seq Scan with Rows Removed by Filter, login p95 hits four seconds, and the fix nobody found for a month is a single expression index on lower(email).

A deploy runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ... without lock_timeout; it queues for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind a 20-minute report SELECT, every subsequent SELECT on orders queues behind the ALTER, the connection pool saturates and the entire application freezes until someone finds the head of the chain with pg_blocking_pids() and terminates it.

A migration script runs CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction on a 200M-row table, holding a SHARE lock that blocks all writes for 40 minutes; the follow-up attempt with CONCURRENTLY is cancelled by a timeout and leaves an INVALID index that is maintained on every write and used by nothing, silently taxing the table for the next year.

PgBouncer in transaction mode sits in front of a FastAPI service whose driver caches prepared statements; the app throws intermittent 'prepared statement "__asyncpg_stmt_12__" does not exist' errors only under load, the team blames the database, and the fix is statement_cache_size=0 or PgBouncer 1.21 with max_prepared_statements.

A job queue uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE LIMIT 1 without SKIP LOCKED, so twenty workers serialise on the first locked row and throughput equals one worker; when someone adds SKIP LOCKED but keeps a composite index ordered (created_at, tenant_id) the queue is fast for small tenants and scans the whole index range for the largest one because the equality column is not leading.

A prepared statement with a tenant_id parameter switches to the generic plan after five executions; the plan chosen for typical 2000-row tenants is a Nested Loop that runs 600000 times for the tenant holding 60% of the data, that one customer times out every hour, and no one connects it to plan_cache_mode because the query is fast every time they run it by hand with a literal.
interviewQuestions: Here is an EXPLAIN ANALYZE: a Nested Loop whose outer Seq Scan was estimated at rows=1 and produced rows=48000, with an inner Index Scan showing loops=48000. Explain why the planner chose this, what you would check in pg_stats, and give three fixes ranked from least to most invasive with the risk of each.

A customer's multi-tenant SaaS has three tenants holding 70% of the rows and two thousand small ones; the same endpoint is 20 ms for small tenants and times out for the big three. Walk me through your diagnosis, covering plan caching and generic plans, statistics targets, partial indexes and partitioning, and tell me what you would actually ship this week and what you would defer.

Design the migration that adds a NOT NULL column with a default, a foreign key to accounts, and a unique index on (tenant_id, external_id) to a two-billion-row table on RDS with no maintenance window. For each step name the lock mode, whether it scans or rewrites, where it can fail, and how your migration runner recovers.

Explain MVCC as Postgres implements it: what an UPDATE physically does, what a HOT update is and what defeats it, how a forgotten idle-in-transaction connection or a replica with hot_standby_feedback causes bloat, and the four numbers you would put on a dashboard to catch it early.

Twenty workers pull jobs from a jobs table. Write the dequeue SQL that is correct under concurrency, explain the lock semantics that make it correct, and then describe what changes if each job triggers a non-idempotent external API call and the process can die between the call and the commit.

When would you choose SERIALIZABLE over explicit row locks, and when the reverse? Describe SSI briefly, the 40001 retry contract that the application must honour, the throughput cost, and give one concrete case for each choice from a system you have built.

A query on a customer database got 100x slower overnight with no deploy and no schema change. Give the first five catalog queries you would run, what each one would tell you, and the three most likely root causes in order of probability.
